id: Man's Short Life and Foolish Ambition

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

In gardens sweet each flower mark did I,How they did spring, bud, blow, wither and die.With that, contemplating of man's short stay,Saw man like to those flowers pass away.Yet built he houses, thick and strong and high,As if he'd live to all Eternity.Hoards up a mass of wealth, yet cannot fillHis empty mind, but covet will he still.To gain or keep, such falsehood will he use!Wrong, right or truth—no base ways will refuse.I would not blame him could he death out keep,Or ease his pains or be secure of sleep:Or buy Heaven's mansions—like the gods become,And with his gold rule stars and moon and sun:Command the winds to blow, seas to obey,Level their waves and make their breezes stay.But he no power hath unless to die,And care in life is only misery.This care is but a word, an empty sound,Wherein there is no soul nor substance found; Yet as his heir he makes it to inherit, And all he has he leaves unto this spirit.To get this Child of Fame and this bare word,He fears no dangers, neither fire nor sword: All horrid pains and death he will endure,Or any thing can he but fame procure. O man, O man, what high ambition growsWithin his brain, and yet how low he goes!To be contented only with a sound,Wherein is neither peace nor life nor body found.

outputs.L1:
Here are two ways to polish the text, depending on your preferred style:

### Option 1: Elevated & Elegant Verse (Preserves poetic structure)

Within sweet gardens, I observed each flower’s fleeting span—
How it did spring, bud, bloom, and fade, much like the life of man.
Contemplating our brief stay, I saw us pass away,
Yet man constructs grand monuments to cheat his own decay.

He builds his fortresses so high, as if eternally to stand,
And hoards great wealth to fill a void no riches can command.
To gain or guard his treasures, he resorts to base deceit,
Forsaking truth and righteousness to harbor his conceit.

I would not judge his desperate quest could gold grant him reprieve—
To banish death, soothe mortal pain, or quiet nights relieve;
Nor if his wealth could purchase heaven, or grant him power divine,
To rule the sun, the moon, the stars, and make the heavens shine;
To calm the storm, command the sea, and bend the wind at will.
Yet man has power but to die; his cares torment him still.

This worldly care is but a sound, an empty, fleeting name,
A hollow ghost to which he leaves his fortune and his fame.
To claim this child of legacy, he braves both fire and sword,
Enduring agony and death for a meaningless reward.

O man, how high ambition grows within your restless mind,
Yet to what depths you stoop to leave all truth and peace behind—
Content to trade a life of grace for nothing but a sound,
Wherein no body, soul, nor peace, nor substance can be found.

---

### Option 2: Eloquent Philosophical Prose (Best for essays, speeches, or formal prose)

Observing the fleeting lifecycles of garden flowers—their emergence, blossom, wilting, and death—I was led to reflect upon the brevity of human existence. Like these blossoms, humanity inevitably fades away. Yet, paradoxically, man constructs formidable structures as though he were immortal, accumulating vast wealth that fails to satisfy his inner emptiness and leaves his desires perpetually unfulfilled. Driven to acquire and preserve his fortune, he stoops to deceit, willingly abandoning morality and truth.

I would not censure his ambition if wealth could truly stave off death, alleviate suffering, guarantee tranquility, or secure heavenly immortality. Nor would I judge him if his riches could grant godlike dominion over the cosmos—commanding the sun, moon, and stars, or mastering the winds and seas. Yet man possesses no such power; his only certainty is mortality, and his ceaseless striving yields only misery. 

This worldly ambition—this pursuit of fame—is an illusion, an empty sound devoid of true substance. Yet man appoints this hollow legacy as his sole heir, sacrificing everything he possesses to it. To secure this fleeting reputation, he braves every danger, enduring fire, sword, intolerable pain, and death itself. How tragic it is that while man harbors such soaring ambitions, he stoops so low, ultimately settling for an ephemeral sound that offers neither peace, nor life, nor genuine substance.
outputs.L2:
While observing a pleasant garden, I watched the lifecycle of blossoms—how they sprouted, bloomed, withered, and ultimately perished. Reflecting on this made me realize that human existence is just as brief and fleeting. 

Despite this brief lifespan, people erect massive, durable, and towering dwellings as though they expect to live eternally. They relentlessly stack up fortunes, yet this wealth fails to satisfy their inner emptiness, leaving them perpetually greedy for more. To acquire or protect their riches, humans willingly embrace deceit and abandon all morality, refusing no wicked or dishonest act. 

I would not fault mankind for these actions if their wealth could actually prevent death, alleviate pain, guarantee restful sleep, or purchase a place in the heavens. Nor would I criticize them if riches allowed them to become like gods—reigning over the celestial bodies, commanding the winds, and flattening stormy ocean waves into calm seas. 

However, mortals possess no such authority; their only certainty is that they will die, and their endless worldly anxieties bring nothing but sorrow. This pursuit of reputation and legacy is merely an empty phrase—a hollow concept containing no real substance or soul. Yet, people treat this illusion as their sole heir, bequeathing everything they own to an unfeeling idea. To secure this meaningless renown, individuals fear no danger, braving fire, weapons, excruciating pain, and even death itself. 

It is astonishing how humanity harbors such lofty aspirations, yet stoops so low—willingly settling for a mere phantom of fame that offers neither peace, physical form, nor true life.
outputs.L3:
**The Vanities of Human Ambition**

Human existence is fundamentally brief and fragile, bound to the same inexorable rhythms that govern the natural world. Like a delicate field flower, a person springs forth from the dust, blooms briefly in the radiance of life, and then inevitably begins to wither beneath the quiet weight of time. In the grand expanse of the universe, a human life is merely a fleeting season—a fragile bloom destined to fade as quickly as it arrived.

Yet, despite the undeniable reality of their mortal nature, human beings remain trapped in a relentless pursuit of worldly gain. Driven by a desperate need for security and status, individuals obsessively hoard wealth, frequently resorting to deceit, betrayal, and moral compromise just to acquire a little more. Tragically, this frantic accumulation yields no true fulfillment. No matter how vast their fortunes grow, their minds remain perpetually empty and unsatisfied, impoverished by constant anxiety and hollowed out by an insatiable desire for *more*.

Ultimately, this obsession with earthly riches and grand ambitions reveals itself as a profound exercise in futility. When confronted with the universal realities of existence, material prosperity proves utterly powerless. No amount of gold, regardless of its measure, possesses the strength to purchase a single extra moment of life, ease the raw agony of suffering, or command the indifferent forces of nature. Death makes no exceptions for the wealthy, and the grave demands an equal surrender from all.

Equally tragic is the human willingness to sacrifice present happiness for the phantom of legacy. Men and women routinely endure extreme danger, severe hardship, and even self-destruction, all to carve their names into the memories of future generations. They trade the precious, quiet reality of their living hours for the illusion of lasting fame. Yet, this hard-won renown is a ghost of a prize—an empty legacy lacking all substance, incapable of offering warmth to the cold ground or bringing genuine light to the soul.

In contemplating these pursuits, one is left to lament the deep, tragic irony of human ambition. It is a heartbreaking spectacle: a species blessed with consciousness chooses to degrade itself and squander its brief moment in the sun, all for illusions that bring neither internal peace nor eternal life. In striving so fiercely to be remembered by a world they must leave behind, humans forget how to truly live.
outputs.L4:
In the quiet stillness of the garden, I watched a solitary bloom unfold its petals to the morning sun. Its beauty was breathtaking, yet by dusk, its edges had frayed, and by week’s end, it had withered into dust. Observing this swift and gentle lifecycle stirred a profound realization within me. The flower did not struggle against its brief existence; it simply bloomed, faded, and returned to the earth. 

Human beings, however, live in perpetual rebellion against the same impermanence. Driven by a deep-seated terror of our own mortality, we refuse to accept the fleeting nature of our lives. Instead, we spend our brief years engaged in a frantic, relentless struggle to outrun the grave. 

Look around, and you will see the evidence of this desperation. Men spend lifetimes hoarding vast fortunes they can never hope to spend, foolishly believing that wealth can purchase immunity from time. They build grand structures—sprawling estates, towering monuments, and vast empires—desperately trying to carve their names into stone so that some memory of them might endure. In this mad pursuit of power, fame, and legacy, moral boundaries crumble. Men willingly commit acts of deceit, betrayal, and cruelty, sacrificing their very souls to secure a temporary throne or a fleeting moment of worldly renown.

Yet, as I returned my gaze to the fallen petals upon the soil, the utter vanity of this human crusade became undeniable. 

For all our grand architecture, accumulated gold, and ruthless conquests, man remains completely powerless against the inexorable approach of death. Nature makes no exceptions for kings, nor does the grave bow to conquerors. The highest empire eventually collapses into ruin, and the wealthy man leaves the world just as naked as the beggar. 

In light of this truth, the frantic striving of humanity is revealed for what it truly is: an empty, self-imposed misery. We trade the quiet joy of the present moment for a feverish dream of immortality that can never be realized. All our ruthless ambition, our hoarded riches, and our grand monuments yield neither lasting substance nor true peace of mind. We exhaust ourselves building castles in the sand, blind to the rising tide that will inevitably wash them—and us—away forever.
outputs.L5:
The art of creation often lies not in the final masterpiece, but in the quiet moments of understanding that precede it. 

I remember sitting on a worn wooden stool in my grandfather’s studio, watching the afternoon sun filter through dust-motes in the air. For years, I had wondered **how** a person could possess such steady hands, effortlessly transforming rough, forgotten blocks of timber into figures that almost seemed to breathe. 

He worked **with** an immense patience, his calloused fingers guiding his chisels across the grain in a slow, deliberate rhythm. To him, the wood was not just a material to be shaped; it was a story waiting to be released. 

Suddenly, he paused and glanced up from his workbench. He **saw** the fascination written across my young face, smiled softly, and handed me a small piece of smooth, polished oak. In that single, shared gesture, I understood that learning to craft isn't just about mastering a technique—it is about learning how to see the potential in everything around you.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a philosophical poem in rhyming couplets using early modern English diction. The speaker should start by observing flowers in a garden to reflect on human mortality, then criticize man's futile pursuit of wealth, power over nature, and empty fame.
counterfactuals.output:
Within this quiet garden's verdant bow'rs,
I mark the fleeting beauty of the flow'rs.
The crimson rose doth blush against the sun,
Yet droops her head before the day is done;
The lily, cloathed in robes of purest white,
Doth yield her fragrance to th’ encroaching night.
Thus Man, a fragile blossom of the dust,
Doth place in earthly days his foolish trust;
He blooms a season in his summer pride,
Then by the scythe of Time is laid aside.

Yet madly doth he crave the yellow ore,
And starves his spirit for a gilded store.
What boots the treasure piled by anxious sighs,
When cold and motionless the miser lies?
Can glittering coin assuage the fevered breath,
Or bribe the stony, silent gates of Death?

He builds high towers to subdue the land,
And dreams to rule the ocean with his hand;
He bends the forest, carves the mountain crest,
Yet earth reclaims him to her darksome breast.
The soil he trod with proud, imperial stride
Doth swallow up his fleeting, hollow pride.

And what is Fame, for which the foolish bleed?
A passing wind, a frail and withered reed.
Though men engrave their names on marble cold,
Time’s rust shall mar what arrogance hath told.
O wretched Man! Learn wisdom from the rose,
Which humbly blooms and unrepining goes;
Lay down thy crown, thy foolish lust for power,
For thou art mortal as the garden flower.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a 17th-century style poem about the futility of human ambition and wealth in the face of death.
counterfactuals.output:
Vain Man, who reared thy palaces of stone,
And spread thy sails upon the restless deep,
Who sat in state upon a gilded throne,
While starving wretches at thy threshold weep:
Know that the Dust which waits thy final breath,
Is deaf to Power, and unbribed by Death.

Thou hoard’st the shining Ore with greedy hand,
And count’st thy treasures by the setting sun,
Yet buy’st no moment in that quiet land,
When thy brief hour of mortal light is done.
Thy rubies pale, thy minted crowns decay,
And all thy riches melt like snow away.

Where now is Caesar and his martial pride?
Where be the robes of royal crimson grain?
The silent skull no pedigree can hide,
The monarch’s bone is as the simple swain’s.
The tyrant's sword, the scholar's subtle ink,
Alike into the grave’s oblivion sink.

The hungry worm cares not for ancient blood,
Nor spares the cheek where rose and lily bloomed;
The marble tomb that reared its head so proud
Serves but to hide the rot that lies entombed.
No trumpet sounds to cheer the sleeping dust,
Where pride is turned to ash, and steel to rust.

Then lay thy foolish scepter in the clay,
And quench the fever of thy vain desire;
For Night encroacheth on thy fleeting Day,
And all thy glory is a dying fire.
Naked we come into this world of care,
And naked to the dark we must repair.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem in the style of Margaret Cavendish or Anne Bradstreet, focusing on the transience of life compared to flowers, and how people obsess over worldly riches and a "bare word" like fame?
counterfactuals.output:
When I behold the Rose in crimson pride,
Which blooms at dawn, and droops by eventide,
Or mark the Lily in her wedding dress,
Whose beauty vanishes in helplessness—
I mourn to see how short a span is given
To all the fairest ornaments of Heaven.
For like the flower that drinks the morning dew,
Man’s fragile days are swift, and very few.
By sudden frost or autumn's chilling breath,
The tender blossom surrenders unto death;
So falls the monarch, so the humble swain,
For flesh is grass, and earthly glory vain.

Yet foolish mortals toil in dust and care,
To heap up riches they can never wear.
We mine the deeps for sparkling ore and gold,
And lock our treasures in a casket cold;
We build fine towers, pretending to defy
The slow, relentless march of time gone by.
Can glinting coin redeem the soul from night,
Or buy one hour of warm, celestial light?
The shroud no pocket holds, the tomb no chest,
To keep the worldly gains by man possessed;
When breath expires, our yellow dirt must stay,
To mock the clay that rots beneath the clay.

And stranger still, we chase a sound, a shade,
And die for praises that must quickly fade.
For what is *Fame*, for which the ambitious strive,
And hazard all to keep a name alive?
'Tis but a *bare word*, tossed upon the air,
A empty phantom, passing false and fair!
A fleeting breath from an uncertain tongue,
A passing echo by the mortal sung.
Will titles carved upon a marble stone
Re-warm the dust or mend the broken bone?
When in the silent dark the body lies,
What boots a "bare word" underneath the skies?

O foolish heart, that trades eternal grace
For short-lived blossoms and a worldly race!
Let greedy minds for shadowy bubbles sigh,
And barter truth for what is doomed to die;
Seek rather wealth that rust cannot decay,
And blossoms blooming in eternal day,
Where Fame is hushed, and earthly riches cease,
Swallowed at last in everlasting peace.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I need a poem comparing human life to a garden flower dying. Make it sound old-fashioned and focus on how pointless it is to hoard money or seek fame when we all die anyway.
counterfactuals.output:
Behold the rose that greets the morning sun,
Arrayed in silk and crowned with drops of dew;
Yet ere the weary march of day is done,
Her petals fall, her beauty fades from view.

So doth the mortal blossom in his hour,
A fragile thing of fleeting, breathless grace;
No spell can stay the wilted garden bower,
Nor arrest the shadows creeping on his face.

What boots it then to heap the glittering gold,
To lock the coffer tight with greedy hand?
Can yellow coin buy back the gathering cold,
Or raise the fallen blossom from the sand?

And what is fame, but breath upon the air?
A hollow song that echoes through the glade;
It cannot shield the monarch from despair,
Nor keep his leaf from turning in the shade.

The king and beggar share the selfsame soil,
Where withered stems and shattered crowns decay;
How foolish is the soul's relentless toil
To hoard the dust that winds shall sweep away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a meditative poem in rhyming couplets where a speaker reflects on how men build grand houses and endure pain just for fame, yet remain powerless against mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
With heavy stone and gilded beam,
Man builds the fortress of his dream,
And raises towers tall and high
To carve his name against the sky.

He bears the scars of toil and pain
To buy a moment of domain,
And bleeds beneath the heavy sun
For glory sought and battles won.

He shapes the arch, he weaves the crest,
To quiet fear within his breast,
Believing vaults of marble hold
A shield against the coming cold.

Yet through the grandest, gated hall,
The unseen shadows slowly fall;
No lordly coat of arms can stay
The quiet stealing of the day.

Though brass be etched with noble praise,
Time counts the cadence of his days,
And softly turns the final page,
Unawed by wealth, unbent by rage.

The pillars crumble into dust,
The iron latches yield to rust;
The earth reclaims what it had lent,
And leaves a silent monument.

How strange that man will bleed for praise,
And burn the candle of his days,
Only to learn, as night draws near,
That fame is but a phantom here.

The wild wind sings, the waters flow,
Long after kings and builders go;
The proudest hall must fall at last,
A breath absorbed into the past.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
